segments.text: I'm here with Scott Kaiser, who is the president of Laser Maintenance Group, and Scott, we're
talking about dominoes the other day and how one thing leads to another thing leads to another
thing. We've got some laser machine parts, I guess, here. Tell me a little bit about what we're
looking at. This is the output coupler. The laser beam exits this optic. 30% of it actually exits
this optic. And the 30% that comes through, it passes through this shroud that's designed
to protect it. This shroud had come off over time. This bolt had backed out or had gotten hot,
and it fell down in front of the output coupler, which created all this damage. As soon as it did
that, it blew pieces of this back onto this, which just about ruined it. There's a crack
right in here that you can see. You can also see through the side, you can see the crystal
cracking in the inside here. This is a pressure boundary. The laser runs at one-tenth of the
atmosphere. So had this imploded, this would have been a half-inch hole straight to atmosphere.
It would have seized the roots blower, probably blown up the power supplies. It would have been
a catastrophic failure. As the beam reflected off of this, it also caught a water line
and melted it, melted it right here and sprayed water over some electrical fittings for the
shutter. We're able to repair that, but it's funny how everything works. But when the beam,
as soon as the beam wasn't passing straight through the beam delivery anymore, it hit the
inside of the tip. You can see all the different colors in it here. The beam should pass through
this hole. It didn't. Instead, it welded the tip shut, which is, now I can't get the laser
beam out, even to the metal, which only a little bit of gas was coming through through these
perimeter holes. But they caught it pretty quick. As soon as they stopped cutting, they
stopped. They stopped the machine. Rather than start it up, raise the power, slow down,
do something. If it's cutting right, everything's okay. But as soon as it quits cutting,
something's changed. So stop, stop and look. If they kept cutting,
cracks inside of here would have made it all the way through. And that would have imploded
this and they'd have lost the resonator. Instead, all the dust is a shroud and an
output cup there and a tip and a few cents worth of hose and some time. That was the
more damaging thing. But at least there was a good lesson to learn. But if something
changes all of a sudden, stop. If you're blowing your maintenance off and letting it go,
and all the machine's still running, just let it go. It's running slower and slower every day.
You're going to end up with something like this, where it just quit running all of a sudden.
And that's why you do routine maintenance. It's to catch problems like this before they
cost you, you know, your resonator. How would the routine maintenance have caught this?
Chances are, this comes off and on as part of the maintenance. If you're doing this right,
this should stay on tight. If you're not, it's hard to get to and it's hard to reach. And
it's a poor design. And chances are, when they put it back on, they just didn't tighten it up
good enough. So that's an example of probably wanting to have qualified people. You know,
that thing sat there for two or three or four or five months. And you know, they should be doing
their maintenance on this type of machine more often than that. Chances are, if you'd have
gotten in there on time and done it, you'd have noticed, oh geez, that was loose and lifted it
right off. And then you could have had an opportunity to talk to the guys and say,
I know that's hard to reach, but if you have the right tool, it's a little easier. But
I have one tool that sits in a dark corner of my toolbox. And the only time it sees the light
a day is to tighten this hole. And it's really hard to get on there tight. What would you have
recommended in terms of routine laser maintenance? How often would you recommend doing that? The
OEM asks for a thousand hour maintenance. Some people are running two shifts, some people
run three, some people run one. A thousand hours would be every six months. These guys run
two shifts a day, but they leave their laser on two 10 hour shifts. So they run 20 hours out of
24 hours. So they hit, they hit their maintenance interval every six weeks. Okay. It's just the
machine's still running. We hate to slow down to stop for that. Well, now you just lost. It's
not so much the cost of this. This was, you know, relatively inexpensive as far as parts go.
It could have been catastrophic, but it's also the time, the two, you know, two days of time
that it took to get in there and then a few hours to fix it and then bring the machine back up.
